newsitem.title: USA: Spaniard pleads innocent to illegal trade with Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Spaniard pleads innocent to illegal trade with Cuba.

text.p: Spanish businessman Francisco Javier Ferreiro-Parga pleaded not guilty on Friday to charges he violated the United States embargo against Cuba by shipping canned food and diapers to the communist-ruled island.
Ferreiro, dressed in prison blues, made a brief court appearance for arraignment on charges of money laundering, conspiracy and violating the U.S. Trading With The Enemy Act.
His Miami attorney, Nathan Diamond, said Ferreiro, 45, was a legitimate businessman who imported goods to Cuba from other countries but not from the United States.
"He's angry about it. He was a tourist in this country. He's very upset with his government for not protecting him," Diamond said outside the Miami federal courthouse.
He was held without bond in a detention centre and his trial should be scheduled within 70 days, prosecutors said.

A federal grand jury indicted Ferreiro on eight counts of violating the U.S. Trading With The Enemy Act, five counts of money-laundering and one count of conspiracy. He faces up to 20 years in prison and fines of up to $1 million, the United States Attorney's Office said.
The United States imposed its economic embargo against President Fidel Castro's communist government more than three decades ago, making it illegal to trade with Cuba.

Prosecutors said Ferreiro shipped groceries, diapers, napkins and other goods under false bills of lading through the Dominican Republic and Curacao to Cuba, where the government sold them to tourist hotels and other businesses.

"Regardless whether he's a citizen of Spain or any other country, he is charged with violating U.S. laws," Wilfredo Fernandez, U.S. Attorney's Office spokesman said. "He knew all along the goods were going to Cuba."
Diamond denied Ferreiro did business in the United States and said his client was the victim of a deal cut by informants who were trying to win lighter sentences in other cases.

According to the indictment, Ferreiro bought goods from Miami-based Central Trading International and shipped them in containers to the Dominican Republic, where they were loaded onto vessels run by Melfi Marine for transport to Ferreiro's Havana-based company, Multi-Import International Holding Co.
In an affidavit, a U.S. Customs agent said Melfi was "a shipping line owned or controlled by the government of Cuba."
Ferreiro also was charged with laundering about $500,000 used in illegal trade with Cuba, prosecutors said.

In Havana, a Foreign Ministry spokesman said on Thursday Cuba was following the case. Jose Ramon Fernandez, deputy president of Cuban's Council of Ministers, said the arrest showed the United States was "trying to terrorise Spanish businessmen so that they don't invest or do business here."

Joaquin de la Herran, Spain's trade commissioner in Miami, said Spanish entrepreneurs did not consider Ferreiro's arrest as an offensive against them. "I think this is a specific case with specific circumstances," he said.
Ferreiro's daughter, Teresa, 22, said her father was innocent and criticised Spain's government.
"I don't know where all of this is coming from. He does no business in the U.S.," she said. "I feel betrayed by justice and by my government. We have received no help from them."
Ferreiro was arrested on April 1 at a shopping mall near where his daughters live on Key Biscayne, an upscale island connected by a causeway to Miami.
